raw.content:
A man in his 80s was brought to the emergency department after a cardiac arrest. According to paramedics, the patient was last seen healthy by his family 4 hours earlier, then was found unresponsive and pulseless in the bathroom. He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, receiving 4 doses of epinephrine intravenously and endotracheal tube intubation with return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 10 minutes. Family later revealed he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and had been complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation. A family member witnessed him struggling for air before losing consciousness.

Initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity.

raw.content:
A woman in her 50s presented with a 2.5-year history of severe urticaria. The primary symptom was chronic pruritus, which was worsening and refractory to treatment. Previous medication trials of doxepin, monteleukast, hydroxizine, famotidine, fexofenadine, and ranitidine provided only minimal benefit. She initially responded well to omalizumab but became refractory after 1 week of treatment.

Examination revealed edematous, superficial wheals and plaques on the arms, back, and thighs, along with dermatographism.

- Skin biopsies: Two 0.4-mm punch biopsies revealed dermal edema with sparse chronic inflammation and dilated blood vessels within the superficial dermis, consistent with dermal hypersensitivity.    - Allergy testing:    - Skin-prick allergy testing was negative    - Food elimination diet results were negative    - Skin patch testing showed positive results for methylisothiazolinones

raw.content:
A 34-year-old Thai man with a history of hypertension and tobacco use disorder, and a family history significant for polycythemia, hypertension, and stroke in his father. He initially presented with worsening bifrontal headaches, nausea, vomiting, and right-sided blurry vision. He was not adherent to his antihypertensive regimen. Three months later, he presented again with right-sided frontal headache, photophobia, tingling in his right fingers, nausea, and vomiting. He reported missing a few doses of his carvedilol and had cut down on his smoking.

Blood pressures in the emergency department ranged from 180 to 190/80-90 mm Hg during initial presentation. On second presentation, systolic blood pressures were 150 to 170 mm Hg. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score was 2 because of complete left homonymous hemianopsia.

- Laboratory tests: Initial presentation showed hemoglobin 20.2 g/dL, hematocrit 54.8%, MCV 74 fL, and thrombocytopenia (91,000/mm³). Second presentation showed hemoglobin 20.1 g/dL, hematocrit 57.2%, MCV 76 fL, and thrombocytopenia (76,000/mm³). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated (21 mm/h). Erythropoietin was normal (7.8 mIU/mL).- Imaging studies:  - CT Head: Left occipital intraparenchymal hemorrhage with intravascular extension (first presentation)  - CT Head: Right posterior parietal intraparenchymal hemorrhage (4.7 × 2.9 × 4.2 cm) with blood product in the right lateral ventricle and minimal midline shift (second presentation)  - MRI Brain: No underlying masses  - Peripheral smear: Showed microcytosis and thrombocytopenia without toxic granulations or blast cells- Hemoglobin Electrophoresis Results:  Hb A: 0.0%  Hb F: 1.7%  Hb A2: 4.4%  Hb E: 34.0%  Hb Tak: 59.9%

A 43-year-old woman with mild intermittent asthma since childhood, well controlled on inhaled fluticasone and salmeterol. Her symptoms started 6 months before presentation, with dyspnea and chronic cough after resolution of a mild COVID-19 infection that didn't require hospitalization. She experienced progressive dyspnea, fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss. She was treated for an asthma exacerbation with a steroid taper without improvement. Seven days before presentation, she developed worsening shortness of breath and new right-sided, pleuritic chest pain.

At presentation:- Afebrile- Mildly tachypneic  - Oxygen saturation of 91% on room air

A 56-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of polyarthralgia over the bilateral wrists, knees, ankles, and left shoulder, associated with early morning stiffness and swelling of the affected joints. Once-daily celecoxib provided significant but incomplete pain relief. He noted diffuse swelling over both feet and ankles and mild puffiness of his left hand. He had no rashes, nail changes, uveitis, or constitutional symptoms. He had a 6-month duration of cough associated with occasional blood streaks, with no previous smoking history.

Synovitis was elicited over both ankles. Bilateral lower limb pitting edema up to the ankles was noted. Reduced breath sounds were heard over the right upper zone. There was no clubbing or cervical lymphadenopathy.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 40.0 mm/h
  - C-reactive protein: 41.0 mg/L
  - Rheumatoid factor: negative
  - Serum creatinine: 73.0 µmol/L (0.83 mg/dL)
  - Serum albumin: 37.0 g/L (within normal range)

- Imaging Studies:
  - Radiographs of hands, knees, ankles, and left shoulder: unremarkable for erosions
  - Chest radiograph: 8.1×6.4-cm mass in the right upper zone
  - Computed tomography of chest: lesion with paratracheal lymphadenopathy
    Image Title: Figure 1
    Image Description: Computed tomography scan of the chest demonstrating a right upper zone mass with paratracheal lymphadenopathy

- Pathology:
  - Endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of mediastinal lymph nodes: ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma with mucinous features

- Additional Studies:
  - Positron emission tomography-computed tomography of full body: small foci suspicious for metastatic disease

A 63-year-old woman presented with difficult-to-treat hypertension. Medical history included bone and central diabetes insipidus diagnosed via femoral biopsy 12 years ago, and liver involvement three years prior that was treated with cytarabine for one year. The patient had untreated dyslipidemia (LDL cholesterol 3.11 mmol/L). She was not a smoker and did not have diabetes. Her body mass index was 19.22 kg/m². No relevant family history was reported. The patient did not report angina, exertional dyspnea, or claudication.

Blood pressure was 198/106 mmHg without orthostatic hypotension or anisosphygmia, and heart rate was 65 beats/min. The cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and a continuous murmur was heard in the epigastric region.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Serum creatinine: 96.36 μmol/L (1.09 mg/dL)    * Potassium: 4.4 mmol/L    * B-type natriuretic peptide: 82,500 pg/mL    * Inflammatory markers: normal    * Urinalysis: unremarkable without albuminuria  - Imaging Studies:    * Transthoracic echocardiogram: left ventricular mass index of 110 g/m² without other relevant changes    * Abdominal CT angiogram:      Title: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT      Description: Right kidney atrophy without discernible right renal artery and high-grade ostial stenosis of the left renal, celiac trunk, and superior mesenteric arteries    * Diethylenetriamine pentaacetate renogram: confirmed right kidney functional exclusion    * Renal vein catheterization: no signs of renin production lateralization

A 71-year-old man presented with three weeks of jaundice, weight loss, abdominal pain, and dark-colored urine. He also reported bilateral lower-extremity weakness that was most noticeable when attempting to arise from a chair, resulting in several ground-level falls. He had no history of autoimmune or neuromuscular conditions. Despite his recent falls, he did not have any prolonged periods of being down that could contribute to muscle injury. He had been taking atorvastatin as a home medication.

Physical findings included:- Jaundice and significant scleral icterus- Epigastric tenderness without guarding or rebound- Mild weakness in bilateral hip flexor muscles

Laboratory Results:- Aspartate aminotransferase: 2536 IU/L- Alanine aminotransferase: 919 IU/L  - Total bilirubin: 169.3 μmol/L- Alkaline phosphatase: 894 IU/L- Creatinine: 415.5 μmol/L (baseline of 70.7 μmol/L three months previously)- Initial creatinine kinase (CK) level: 22,000 IU/L, later peaked at >40,000 IU/L- Cancer antigen 19-9 level: 2930 kU/LImaging Studies:- CT abdomen/pelvis: 2.6 × 3.1 cm pancreatic head mass with associated pancreatic ductal dilatation, without evidence of metastatic disease- MRI: Diffuse myositis affecting lower extremities  Image Description: Axial and coronal views showing diffuse symmetrical hyperintense signal highly suggestive of diffuse myositisPathology:- Pancreatic head biopsy: Hypocellular with scant atypical cells- Biliary stricture biopsy: Consistent with adenocarcinoma- Right biceps femoris biopsy: Nonspecific myopathic changes consistent with rhabdomyolysis- BiliSeq genetic sequencing: Demonstrated genomic alterations in targeted regions of genes involved in biliary-tract malignancies

A 22-year-old Japanese man (BMI: 22.7 kg/m²) with no medical history or family history developed fever and erythema on trunk and extremities 3 days after receiving first dose of Moderna vaccine. On the 12th day after second vaccination, he developed fever. Initial symptoms gradually worsened leading to hospitalization on the 24th day after second vaccination. After initial discharge, he was readmitted for chest pain.

Initial presentation included fever and erythema on the trunk and extremities. During readmission, patient presented with chest pain that was refractory and persistent.

Laboratory Tests (Initial admission):- C-reactive protein: 19.77 mg/dL (normal, <0.15 mg/dL)- Leukocyte count: 12,480/μL (normal, 3,500−9,700/μL)- Platelet count: 271 × 10³/μL (normal, 140−379 × 10³/μL)- Serum ferritin: 443.1 ng/mL (normal, 21−282 ng/mL)- D-dimer: 1.1 µg/mL (normal, <1.0 µg/mL)Laboratory Tests (Readmission):- High-sensitivity troponin I: 6327 pg/mL (normal, <26.2 pg/mL)- Creatine phosphokinase: 325 U/L (normal, 38−196 U/L)- D-dimer: 1.6 µg/mL- Platelet count: 87 × 10³/μLImaging Studies:1. Initial contrast-enhanced CT:- Revealed hepatosplenomegaly- Contrast-enhanced defective area in kidney2. Coronary angiography:- Total occlusion of atrioventricular branch of right coronary artery- 90% stenotic lesions with >3 mm coronary ectasia in left circumflex artery3. Optical coherence tomography:- Showed blurring of intravascular structure- Intimal thickening- Medial vessel destruction- Thrombi in RCA and LCx lesions4. Follow-up contrast-enhanced CT:- New intrahepatic arterial luminal irregularities- Enlarged contrast-enhanced defective area in kidneySARS-CoV-2 PCR test results were repeatedly negative

raw.content:
An 81-year-old man initially developed a cough, subjective fever, and shortness of breath. He was first treated with azithromycin for bronchitis, followed by levofloxacin after a right upper lobe infiltrate was found. His symptoms progressed despite antibiotics. Medical history includes coronary artery disease with coronary artery bypass (two years prior), atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c: 8.1%). He had spent time at a Northern Minnesota cabin but reported minimal outdoor exposure. Previous missionary work in Colombia ended two years before admission. Never smoked and rarely consumed alcohol.

Vital signs: Temperature 38.6°C, Pulse 130 beats/min, Blood Pressure 114/61 mm Hg, Respiratory Rate 22 breaths/min, Oxygen Saturation 82% (improved to >90% with 5 L/min oxygen). Lung sounds were diminished in the right upper lobe, with diffuse crackles in the right lung base. No clubbing or cyanosis. Cardiac examination showed tachycardic irregularly irregular rhythm, systolic ejection murmur, and mild pitting edema to the knee bilaterally. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Neurologic and skin examinations were normal. Later developed right-sided ptosis and anisocoria with an asymmetrically miotic right pupil (more evident in dark environment).

Laboratory Tests:
- Leukocytosis: 15,000/mm³
- Procalcitonin: 0.77 ng/mL
- Positive Blastomyces urine antigen
- Positive Histoplasmosis blood antigen
- Negative results for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
- Negative antigen tests for Cryptococcus, Legionella, and influenza
- Negative Paracoccidioides serum antibody

Imaging Studies:
1. Chest Radiograph
Title: Initial Chest Radiograph
Description: Dense consolidation of the right upper lobe, patchy nodular infiltrates of left upper lobe, 5-mm noncalcified rounded infiltrate in posterolateral left lower lobe

2. CT and MRI
Title: Emergency Head CT and Brain MRI
Description: Both showed no acute process

Other Tests:
Bronchoscopy findings: Moderate clear secretions with erythematous and edematous bronchial mucosa
Bronchoalveolar lavage: Spherical broadly based budding yeast on Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stain

raw.content:
A 71-year-old patient with recurrent stage IIIC papillary serous adenocarcinoma of the ovary. Initial treatment included resection and 6 cycles of adjuvant paclitaxel/carboplatin. One year later, the patient developed liver and cecal metastases. Over the next seven years, the patient underwent multiple treatments and developed metastases to the right pleura, abdominal masses, and new liver and splenic metastases. The patient was negative for germline mutation but positive for somatic mutation.

No specific physical examination findings were detailed in the case report.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a five-day history of left scrotal soreness and oedema. The patient had no lower urinary tract symptoms and no major relevant medical or surgical history. Based on penile characteristics, the patient was diagnosed with occult penis. Other congenital anomalies of the genitourinary tract were excluded based on imaging findings.

Scrotal investigation revealed an enlarged testis, epididymis, and infected appendages. No torsion was evident in the sperm vessels; however, purulent foci were visible on the surface of the vessels, and their texture was tough and inseparable. The patient was at Tanner stage G4P4.

- Laboratory tests: Blood workup showed mild leukocytosis (18.5 × 109/L). Urine analysis was negative. Pus culture isolated P. aeruginosa, susceptible to ceftazidime and ofloxacin.- Imaging studies:  1. Doppler ultrasonography: Revealed an enlarged left testis with heterogeneous echo pattern, enhanced vascularity, and retained testicular blood flow.  2. Follow-up sonography: Showed heterogeneous echotexture in the left testis and epididymis, with a mild whirlpool sign and hyperechogenicity in the inguinal area.  3. MRI Image (at 60 days):     Title: MR imaging of testes     Description: Left testis showed no enhancement in T2, indicating disappearance of the left testis.- Pathological examination: Showed hemorrhagic infarction of the left testicular appendage and fibrocystic-like tissue with inflammatory cell infiltration.

A 39-year-old male patient was admitted to hospital with recurrent post-activity chest pain and shortness of breath for more than 11 years and bilateral lower extremity edema for one week in March 2021. His symptoms began in 2010 when he first experienced post-activity chest pain and shortness of breath for half a year. The patient was initially acyanotic from 2010 to 2016, but gradually became cyanotic after an episode of severe cough and hemoptysis (approximately 50ml in volume) following a severe cold leading to pneumonia in July 2016.

The patient presented with mild bilateral lower extremity edema. Femoral artery oxygen saturation was measured at 88.5% (decreased from a previous measurement of 93.4% in 2016).

raw.content:
A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.

Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative.

- Histopathologic examination:    Image A: Clinical image of annular arc from a longitudinally furrowed skin lesion on the left eyebrow and forehead to an alopecic lesion    Image B: Clinical image of the bandlike grooved alopecic lesion on the left side of the frontal scalp and vertex    Image C: Scanning view shows predominant lymphocytic infiltrates in perifollicular and periappendageal regions of the dermis and lobular panniculitis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)    Image D: High-power view shows inflammatory infiltrates between adipocytes with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)  - Laboratory findings:    - Direct immunofluorescence: Positive with granular deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen in the dermal blood vessels    - Antinuclear antibody: Negative    - Antidouble-stranded DNA antibody: Negative    - All other laboratory test findings were normal

raw.content:
A woman in her 40s presented with blurred vision in the right eye. She was undergoing treatment with systemic steroids, durvalumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor), and bevacizumab. Ten days after initial presentation, the patient developed sudden vision loss in the right eye.

Initial examination: Visual acuity of 20/25 OU. Right eye showed full visual field, right-sided relative afferent pupillary defect, unremarkable anterior segment, and mild swelling of the optic disc. Left eye had normal fundus and visual function. Follow-up examination (after vision loss): Right eye showed no light perception vision, marked swelling of the optic disc, peripapillary retinal hemorrhages, and occlusion of the superior branch artery. Two days later: Combined occlusion of the central retinal artery and vein, and a new collection of whitish material suspended anterior to the optic disc, forming a pocket in the posterior vitreous.

- Imaging Studies:    Image Title: MRI at Onset of Vision Loss    Image Description:     - Coronal T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Focal enhancement along enlarged right optic nerve    - Axial T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Diffuse enlargement of orbital portion of right optic nerve, enhancement of nerve sheath, slight flattening of posterior globe    - Coronal T2-weighted (FLAIR) image: Hyperintensity of right optic nerve  - Laboratory Tests:    - Lumbar puncture showed no abnormalities      - Other Tests:    - Wide-field fluorescein angiography: Showed choroidal flush but complete lack of perfusion of retinal vasculature      - Pathological Examination:    - Vitreous biopsy: Hypercellular sample with astrocytic neoplasm, small to medium-sized cells with scant cytoplasm and oval, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei    - Immunohistochemistry: Positive for glial fibrillary acid protein, oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2, mutant IDH-1 protein, p53; Loss of ATRX protein; Ki-67 proliferation index ~10%

A 50-year-old male patient was brought to the emergency department due to syncope 30 minutes before admission. The patient reported experiencing palpitation and amaurosis, followed by loss of consciousness that lasted for several minutes, without any preceding body position change, cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath. The patient experienced a previous episode of syncope 1 month prior. Medical history indicated only diabetes, which was well controlled with medication.

Patient was alert and asymptomatic, with vital signs: blood pressure 125/96 mm Hg, pulse rate 81 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% under ambient air. Physical examination showed normal results.

- Laboratory Tests: Blood glucose, electrolytes, D-dimer, troponin I (<0.01 ng/mL), and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide were normal.- Cardiac Tests:  - Electrocardiogram: Initially normal  - Transthoracic echocardiography: Normal, with left ventricular ejection fraction of 58%  - 12-lead 24-hour Holter monitoring: Recorded polymorphic ventricular tachycardia during presyncope episode, with QTc of 403 milliseconds    Image Title: 12-Lead Holter Monitoring    Image Description: ST-segment elevation and fusion with R waves in leads I, aVL, and V1 to V5, followed by short bursts of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia- Coronary Angiography:   - 50% to 90% diffuse stenosis in proximal to mid-LAD  - 80% stenosis in mid-right coronary artery  - Intravascular ultrasonography showed minimum lumen area of 5.92 mm2 in proximal LAD, with plaque burden of 74%

raw.content:
A woman in her 50s presented with 4 days of blurry vision and pain in her left eye after undergoing a routine dental cleaning 1 week prior. She had no history of gingival disease or cavities. Her medical and ocular histories were unremarkable.

Visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/50 OS. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Left eye examination showed conjunctival hyperemia, faint keratic precipitates, 3+ cells with fibrin in the anterior chamber, mild nuclear sclerosis, and a whitish focal granuloma at the 4-o'clock position at the pupillary margin. The posterior segment was unremarkable, with no evidence of vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis. The right eye was unremarkable. At 1-day follow-up, visual acuity declined to 20/100 OS, with development of hypopyon and increased fibrinous material emanating from the iris lesion. No posterior segment involvement was noted.

- Microscopy: Gram stain revealed gram-positive cocci in chains and gram-positive rods in a branching pattern.  Image Title: Gram Stain of Iris Abscess  Image Description: Mixed flora of gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains and gram-positive bacilli (original magnification ×400)- Cultures: Aerobic culture revealed Streptococcus intermedius. The gram-positive bacilli could not be identified more specifically.- Additional Tests: Blood and urine cultures, electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were unremarkable.

raw.content:
A 13-year-old boy presented with an intensely pruritic skin eruption that appeared approximately 24 hours after intensive sun exposure in spring. The patient was otherwise healthy but reported an episode of malaise and headache 2 weeks before first presentation. He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers.

Erythema and helical thickening as well as numerous small blisters, 2 to 3 mm in diameter, were present on both ears. Similar vesicles were observed at the upper and lower vermillion border. Several erythematous papules and crusts were located on the cheeks, neck, and lower arms.

- Laboratory tests: Differential blood count, routine chemical analysis, and serum porphyrins were unremarkable. Serum parvovirus B19 (PVB19) IgM and IgG antibodies were detectable. Bacterial cultures from blister fluid were unremarkable.- Virologic analyses: Negative results for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis B and C viruses, 8 human polyomaviruses, and enteroviruses. PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen, but not in the serum.- Other tests: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable.- Images:  Image 1 Title: The Patient's Clinical Findings on the Ears at First Presentation  Image 1 Description: Helical thickening, erythema, and numerous small vesicles are present on both ears  Image 2 Title: The Patient's Facial Lesions  Image 2 Description: Crusted papules and small erosions are located on the cheeks. Several blisters are located at the upper and lower vermillion border

raw.content:
A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Patient had undergone left-sided mastectomy 2.5 years prior and had been on anastrozole therapy for more than 2 years. Medical history and past medication use were otherwise unremarkable.

Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/150 OS without improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were normal. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. No inflammation in the periphery was noted in either eye.

- Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):  Image Title: OCT Scans  Image Description: Right eye showed significant cystoid macular edema and subfoveal fluid. Left eye had a mild epiretinal membrane.- Fluorescein Angiography:  Image Title: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography  Image Description: Revealed cystoid macular edema with leakage in both right and left eyes.- Blood Tests: Tests for vasculitis and rheumatologic disorders were within reference limits. Normal findings for tick-borne and bacterial diseases.- Imaging:  Computed tomography of the chest was unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 36-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a live-related renal transplant 6 months ago and has been maintained on tacrolimus 3.5 mg daily, mycophenolate sodium 720 mg daily, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. He presented with a 14-day history of low-grade fever, dry cough, and anorexia without dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, or weight loss. He was afebrile on admission, heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral inspiratory crackles; other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; total lymphocyte count 9900/μL; absolute neutrophil count 7720/μL; platelets 285 000/μL; serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated PaO₂ 68 mm Hg and an A–a gradient of 22 mm Hg. HIV ELISA was negative. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities without pleural or mediastinal abnormalities.

Sputum induction was non-diagnostic. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii on Grocott’s methenamine silver stain and negative for acid-fast bacilli, CMV inclusion bodies, and fungal hyphae. He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and a prednisone taper, with clinical and radiographic resolution of infiltrates after 2 weeks.

Three weeks into therapy, he was asymptomatic except for an occasional dry cough. TMP-SMX was discontinued, and prednisolone was maintained at 10 mg daily. Laboratory studies then showed leukopenia (TLC 1400/μL; ANC 1050/μL). Chest radiograph revealed new left upper-zone infiltrates. Repeat HRCT showed resolution of ground-glass opacities and new patchy peribronchovascular consolidations in the right upper lobe, left upper lobe, and left lower-lobe apical segment. Repeat BAL was negative for AFB, fungus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. 

Transbronchial lung biopsy from the left upper lobe showed alveoli filled with inflammatory debris consisting of granulation tissue, interstitial inflammation, and areas of intra-alveolar fibrin deposition.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bipolar disorder was admitted for a 4-week history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, and a 7-kg weight loss, with vomiting during the last 2 days. On examination, her BMI was 18.2 kg/m2 and she was obnubilated; the ECG was normal. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum calcium 3.8 mmol/L (normal phosphorus), nonregenerative normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and acute functional renal failure (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min).  
• PTH 9 ng/L.  
• Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; negative 24-hour proteinuria; no monoclonal peak on serum or urine immunoelectrophoresis; normal serum free light-chain ratio.  

She received IV saline and one dose of zoledronate, with normalization of calcium and renal function by day 3. A CT scan of the body showed two osteolytic lesions of the left frontal and temporal skull bones, multiple hypodense micronodules in all hepatic segments, and multiple splenic nodules. Brain MRI demonstrated T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the same skull regions. A DEXA scan revealed osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score –2.4). Mammography, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy and labial salivary gland histology were unremarkable. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of the liver showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis without malignancy. The intradermal tuberculin test was negative. During this period, hypercalcemia recurred, and two additional doses of zoledronate were administered 15 days apart despite initial correction.

A 34-year-old man with hypertension on dual antihypertensive therapy, well followed by nephrology, presented to the emergency department with acute onset epigastric pain. He described the pain as continuous, burning, non-radiating, and of moderate intensity. His blood pressure was 200/84 mm Hg; all other vital signs were normal. On examination, he had epigastric tenderness without other abnormalities. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with signs of left ventricular hypertrophy. Routine blood tests, including troponin, were normal. While awaiting laboratory results, a point-of-care ultrasound was performed to evaluate the gallbladder; it showed a normal gallbladder without gallstones, no wall thickening, and no pericholecystic fluid. Subsequent cardiac windows revealed a small pericardial effusion.

A 33-year-old man with a history of massive small-bowel and ileocecal resection 12 years earlier (leaving 40 cm of small intestine) was maintained on a normal diet after bowel rehabilitation. One month before admission, he developed diarrhea and a 7-kg weight loss with progressive weakness, anorexia, dizziness, and cachexia. On admission his weight was 36 kg (BMI 12.2 kg/m^2), heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 bpm. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed pitting edema of the lower extremities, thin skin, a scaphoid abdomen, and no ascites. Chest radiography revealed a dense nodule outside the right upper lung field (thought to be rib calcification). Lower-limb radiographs and renal ultrasonography were normal; gallbladder ultrasonography showed atrophy. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening/inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and an incomplete right bundle-branch block. Initial laboratory values included: phosphate 1.10 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.60 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, albumin 27.7 g/L, prealbumin 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin 48 g/L, hematocrit 14.0%, BUN 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 86 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with severe malnutrition and received blood transfusion; parenteral nutrition (500 kcal/day); fluids; electrolyte, trace-element, and multivitamin supplementation (including daily thiamine 100 mg IV). Over 24 hours his strength and edema improved. Then he acutely developed profound fatigue and flaccid weakness of all four limbs. His heart rate was 98 bpm, respiratory rate was unchanged, and repeat labs showed a phosphate level of 0.05 mmol/L.

A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history was noted by his parents to have a slowly developing limitation in right-eye movement over several weeks. There was no pain, inflammation, fever, trauma, or history of ocular infection, and his overall health was unchanged. On examination, abduction of the right eye was restricted. There were no signs of proptosis, strabismus, visual impairment, or inflammation in either eye; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including an infectious work-up, were negative.  
Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a well-circumscribed extraconal mass at the right superolateral orbital wall, adjacent to the frontozygomatic suture, with smooth bone remodeling and fluid-attenuating content but no bone invasion. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a cystic mass in the right superior extraconal compartment that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on FLAIR imaging, and exhibited no diffusion restriction or internal enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion exerted mild compression on the external and superior rectus muscles, correlating with the abduction deficit, but did not involve the optic nerve, intraconal fat, or show intracranial extension.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of vague, colicky epigastric pain radiating to the interscapular region, associated with anorexia and malaise. The pain was relieved by changes in sitting position and worsened by eating. There was no history of alcohol use, abdominal trauma, or pancreatitis. Routine laboratory studies showed thrombocytosis (platelet count >1 000 000/µL) and elevated blood urea. Aspirin (80 mg daily) was initiated for presumed essential thrombocytosis. 

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a cystic lesion in the head of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a well-circumscribed, 11.8 cm cystic mass in the pancreatic head, without invasion of adjacent organs or lymphadenopathy. The serum CA 19-9 level was within the normal range. 

On physical examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation but no rebound or rigidity. There were no signs of portal hypertension or history of prior abdominal surgery.

A 35-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder and chronic joint pain presented with a 15-month history of swelling and redness of her hands. She reported no precipitating factors, including temperature changes. She had occupational exposure to pool chemicals but noted no improvement with glove use. She described chronic joint pain in her hands and back. Prior treatments with topical mupirocin and emollients were unsuccessful. She denied coagulopathy but endorsed a 4-year history of injecting heroin, buprenorphine, suboxone, and morphine without tourniquet use into multiple sites, including the dorsal hands, wrists, and forearms. Three years after cessation of intravenous drug use, she experienced intermittent, painless, symmetric swelling of both hands. Two years later, during the second trimester of pregnancy, she developed persistent hand and foot edema with new erythema and was hospitalized for cardiac and thrombosis evaluation. An echocardiogram showed a normal ejection fraction; no diagnosis was made. Eleven months postpartum, examination revealed bilateral dorsal hand erythema and edema sharply demarcated at the wrists. Punch biopsy showed small‐vessel ectasia and minimal perivascular lymphocytes. Laboratory studies demonstrated negative antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen panel, and rheumatoid factor. Creatine kinase and aldolase were mildly elevated. Six-month–old creatinine levels, hepatic function tests, and hepatitis panels were normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 44-year-old woman from Veracruz, Mexico, of low socioeconomic status, with systemic lupus erythematosus since 2003 (cutaneous, joint, and renal involvement), presented with a one-week history of progressive headache, phonophobia, high-grade fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. One month earlier, she had been treated for SLE-associated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with plasmapheresis, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone at 1 mg/kg per day.

On admission she had systemic inflammatory response syndrome and nuchal rigidity but no focal neurologic deficits or clinical signs of lupus activity. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 103 fL, eosinophils 150 cells/mm3, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, haptoglobin 77 mg/dL, ALT 59 IU/L, AST 78 IU/L, LDH 310 mg/dL, C3 96.5 mg/dL, lactate 0.9 mmol/L, and proteinuria 310 mg/day. Chest radiograph and head CT were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed a pH of 7.35, glucose 45 mg/dL (serum glucose 130 mg/dL), protein 329 mg/dL, 42 white cells/mm3 (95% neutrophils), and 2 red cells/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grew Enterococcus gallinarum, and she was treated with intravenous ampicillin, with improvement in her neurologic symptoms.

On hospital day 3, she developed hemoptysis, bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph, a drop in hemoglobin concentration, and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU admission. Cultures were obtained, and she was started on methylprednisolone boluses and broad-spectrum antibiotics. The initial clinical diagnosis was diffuse alveolar hemorrhage caused by SLE activity without sufficient clinical criteria of nosocomial pneumonia.

On hospital day 4, she developed a purpuric skin rash, and a skin biopsy was performed.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 38-year-old Indian man with a history of recurrent low-grade fevers and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus treated with metformin presented with 10 days of right-sided chest and right upper abdominal pain and dyspnea. He described sharp, tearing, localized pain (7/10), worsened by movement and deep inspiration, without cough or hemoptysis. He denied gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, sick contacts, recent travel, or asbestos exposure. He reported past extramarital sexual relationships. On admission: temperature 37.2°C; heart rate 110 bpm; blood pressure 130/80 mmHg; respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Examination revealed a patchy, macular hyperpigmented rash on both shins and dorsum of the feet, and decreased breath sounds and vocal fremitus at the right lower chest. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 12.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 15 g/dL, platelets 219 × 10^3/µL; blood urea nitrogen 4.3 mmol/L; creatinine 69 µmol/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated patchy infiltrates in the right lower zone and obliteration of the right costophrenic angle. Thoracentesis yielded pale yellow fluid with 1260 WBCs/µL (87% neutrophils), 1590 RBCs/µL, pH 7.237; a rare giant cell was seen; cultures were negative. Pleural biopsy showed empyema without granulomas; Quantiferon and acid-fast bacilli studies were negative. CT chest revealed multiple encysted pleural effusions in the right lung. Transesophageal echocardiography showed no thrombi or intracardiac masses. A comprehensive respiratory viral and atypical pathogen panel was negative. The patient was treated sequentially with piperacillin/tazobactam and then meropenem, with gradual resolution of fever and clinical improvement; a chest tube and thoracotomy were performed to drain the effusion.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of gradually progressive swelling, pain, and stiffness in her left lower leg. She reported pain at rest and denied fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, or syncope. Her medical history was notable for three prior abortions, recurrent microcytic anemia treated with iron supplementation, and two prior dilation and curettage procedures. She had no personal history of DVT and no family history of thromboembolic disease.

On examination, her temperature was afebrile, heart rate 85 bpm, blood pressure 125/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. The left lower leg was tender, swollen, warm, and erythematous. A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history. 

On examination, there were seven subcutaneous, nontender, mobile swellings measuring 1×1 to 3×3 cm in the cervical regions, right paraspinal area, and anterior abdominal wall. The lesions were firm to hard without changes in the overlying skin. 

Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal). 

Cytology smears from all sites showed moderate cellularity with similar features: predominantly plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fragments of collagenous matrix, and occasional small cells with scant cytoplasm. The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. Nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, or atypicality was not seen, and mitoses were sparse. There was no necrosis or inflammatory cells. 

Ultrasonography confirmed that all lesions were confined to the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy or deeper masses.

raw.content:
A 14-year-old Caucasian girl was transferred from a community emergency department after treatment for presumed anaphylaxis following ingestion of a hypoallergenic nutritional supplement. Immediately after ingestion she reported wheezing, cough, and swelling of the lips, face, and tongue and self-administered epinephrine (0.3 mg) at home. Her history included suspected food allergies (wheat, oats, tree nuts, chocolate, eggs, cow’s milk, and rice) without documented reactions; intermittent asthma; complex regional pain syndrome; delayed gastric emptying; and major depressive disorder treated with fluoxetine, increased to 60 mg daily 5 months earlier. Skin prick tests and serum-specific IgE to foods of concern were negative except for sensitization to several tree nuts without a supportive history of reaction with ingestion. Testing for hereditary angioedema and baseline serum tryptase were normal. She had lost 40 lb over the past year through dietary restriction and exercise and was homeschooled due to fears of allergic reactions.

In the ED she had stridor, biphasic wheezing, and poor air movement without visible oropharyngeal swelling. She was afebrile, blood pressure 94/48 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min, and SpO₂ 100% on room air. She received IV fluids, two doses of subcutaneous epinephrine, inhaled bronchodilators, racemic epinephrine, and antihistamines, and was admitted to the PICU. Her presumed angioedema resolved with treatment.

Over the next several weeks in an eating-disorder program, she had seven similar episodes requiring ED evaluation and PICU admission. Each episode featured subjective perioral swelling, hypotension within her baseline range, and stridor that resolved without objective edema. Direct laryngoscopy during one episode showed no airway edema or paradoxical vocal cord motion. Serial serum tryptase levels during acute events remained normal, a bone marrow biopsy was equivocal, and further workup—including complement levels, mast cell mediators, urine prostaglandins, complete blood count, and metabolic panel—was unremarkable. She was managed with daily antihistamines, ranitidine, cromolyn, and a tapering course of prednisone; rescue therapy included cetirizine and lorazepam. She continued to experience suicidal ideation and auditory hallucinations and was started on aripiprazole.

raw.content:
A 56-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presented with a six-day history of progressive swelling of the left labia, which ruptured and began draining serosanguinous fluid two days before admission. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg despite intravenous fluid resuscitation, pulse 96‒100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.4 × 10^9/L. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated, and a surgical consultation was obtained. Pelvic CT imaging demonstrated an ulceration of the left labia with air in the subcutaneous fat of the left groin and lower abdominal wall, as well as inflammatory fat stranding along the left lateral abdominal wall. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was calculated as 3, with the potential to rise to 7 pending C-reactive protein results. Despite non-definitive laboratory and imaging findings, concerns for sepsis, subcutaneous gas on CT, and the LRINEC score led to the decision to proceed with immediate exploratory surgery.

raw.content:
A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of burning on urination, urinary frequency, nocturia, and constant 5/10 suprapubic pain that did not radiate. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, weight change, palpitations, heat or cold intolerance, peripheral edema, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was one week earlier. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the para-umbilical area, without costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory tests showed a negative serum β-hCG, normal CBC and BMP, and a urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites; cervical NAAT was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A diagnosis of lower urinary tract infection was made, and she received a 10-day course of antibiotics as an outpatient.

Despite treatment, her dysuria, frequency, and burning worsened. She reported chronic constipation, with two hard, non-bloody stools per week managed intermittently with stool softeners. There was no history of abdominal trauma or family gastrointestinal disease. 

Because of persistent symptoms, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus, with surrounding acute inflammatory stranding and minimal fluid. There was possible invasion into the bladder dome, secondary thickening of an adjacent distal small-bowel loop, and perivesical stranding around a thick-walled, collapsed bladder.

Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

raw.content:
A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with severe left knee pain and bilateral genu valgum deformity. She recalls being told she “may have had rickets” at age 9 but was lost to follow-up. At 22, she had trochanteric bursitis and an X-ray showed a Q-angle of 17°; no metabolic evaluation was done. She takes OTC vitamin D3 without calcium. She is 155 cm tall, weighs 58.5 kg (BMI 23.8), with no personal or family history of fractures or metabolic bone disease.

On exam, there is marked bilateral valgus alignment (left > right) with a knocking gait. Repeat X-ray shows a Q-angle of 23°. Bone density scanning reveals osteopenia of the left femoral head and normal lumbar spine density. Laboratory studies show:
• Serum phosphate: low  
• Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D: elevated  
• Parathyroid hormone: low  
• FGF23: undetectable  

A 24-hour urine collection demonstrates inappropriately normal phosphate excretion for the degree of hypophosphatemia and normal urine calcium. Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis without stones.

A 49-year-old woman of African origin presented with a 10-year history of a right‐sided scalp mass that had been stable and nontender until it was excised at a peripheral clinic 5 months ago (no histopathology was done). Over the next 5 months, the lesion recurred, gradually enlarged, ulcerated, and bled easily. She denied headaches, convulsions, or neurologic deficits. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was no pallor, jaundice, or palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Local scalp examination revealed two lesions on the right side: a fungating, tender, 9 × 7 cm mass prone to bleeding and mild mobility, and a second non‐fungating, 3 × 3 cm lesion. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and basic metabolic panel. Chest radiography and abdominal/pelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. A head and neck CT scan demonstrated a multilobulated, hyperdense, ulcerative right frontal scalp lesion measuring 9 × 7.8 × 6 cm without skull bone erosion or intracranial extension, along with enlarged cervical lymph nodes at levels I and II. MRI of the spine revealed a pathological compression fracture of T10 and a hyperintense lesion in T8, raising suspicion for vertebral metastases. Clinical staging was considered stage IVc.

raw.content:
A 56-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-week history of dry cough and mild weight loss. She denied fever, haemoptysis, night sweats, and had no known contacts with tuberculosis. Two courses of antibiotics produced no improvement. On examination, coarse crepitations were heard over the right upper and lower lung zones. A chest radiograph showed an air-space opacity in the right upper lobe. CT of the thorax demonstrated multifocal consolidations in the right upper lobe extending to the right lower lobe. Given the clinical and radiographic suspicion for pulmonary tuberculosis, she was started empirically on anti-tuberculosis therapy. After 2 weeks, her symptoms persisted. A Mantoux tuberculin skin test showed 10 mm of induration. Sputum induction for acid-fast bacilli was negative, and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Xpert® Mycobacterium tuberculosis/rifampicin assay as well as bacterial and fungal cultures. Hence, a CT-guided lung biopsy was planned.

raw.content:
A 9-year-old boy was referred with left cheek swelling and hyperglobus of the left eye. Hyperglobus was first noted about 1 year earlier under ophthalmologic observation. Six months later, swelling of the left cheek developed, with marked progression over the preceding 3 months. 

On extraoral examination, there was a painless, bony-hard swelling of the left cheek. The overlying skin was normal, but the patient reported numbness of the left cheek and weakness in movement of the left upper lip. There were no other neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, and ocular motility was intact. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of the left maxillary ridge with mobility of primary teeth c, d, and e.

A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, expansile, heterogeneous (mixed-density) mass occupying the entire left maxillary sinus. The lesion caused deviation and destruction of the nasal septum, invaded the ethmoid sinus, thinned, displaced, and perforated the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, extended into the pterygopalatine fossa with destruction of the pterygoid plates, and elevated and perforated the left infraorbital rim. There was extreme postero-superior displacement of the second molar toward the inferior orbital fissure, resulting in blockage of the fissure, and compromise of the nasopharyngeal space.

Medical history was notable for seasonal allergic reactions and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; blood pressure was documented as 10/5 mmHg. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed WBC 19 × 10³/μl, RBC 3.66 × 10⁶/μl, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dl, hematocrit 33.2%, and MCHC 31.9 g/dl; other serum chemistries were normal.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with mepivacaine to minimize the risk of methemoglobinemia.

raw.content:
A 59‐year‐old Japanese woman was referred for 6 weeks of bilateral posterior ankle pain and anterior knee pain, and 4 weeks of pain in the metacarpophalangeal joint of the left third finger. She had been diagnosed with hypertension and heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) at age 57, with an initial LDL‐C of 359 mg/dL, reduced to ~170 mg/dL on pitavastatin and ezetimibe for the past 6 months. She had no personal or family history of rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, she had bilateral arcus corneae; swelling and thickening of the midportion of both Achilles tendons with tenderness to palpation extending to the calcaneal insertion; tenderness over both tibial tuberosities and the right medial humeral epicondyle; and tenderness of the first and fifth right MTP joints and the second left MTP joint. The right third and right second MCP joints were swollen dorsally, and a nodule was noted on the extensor tendon of the right third digit. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 118 mm/h, CRP 2.06 mg/dL, rheumatoid factor 49.3 U/mL (normal <15), anti‐CCP2 >300 U/mL (normal <4.5), and MMP‐3 62.3 ng/mL (normal <59.7). Radiographs of the hands, feet, ankles, and knees showed no erosions or enthesophytes, although the ankle films demonstrated soft‐tissue widening suggestive of Achilles tendon thickening. Musculoskeletal ultrasound revealed the following:
- Achilles tendons: markedly swollen, rounded cross‐section; inhomogeneous, hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed markedly increased vascularity inside and around the tendon, with vessels entering from the ventral aspect via Kager’s fat; no paratenon thickening, bursitis, or bony irregularity.  
- Patellar tendons: focal thickening of the distal tendon, inhomogeneous hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed increased flow in hypoechoic areas; no bursitis or bony changes; mild suprapatellar synovitis.  
- Finger extensor tendons at the right third and left second and fourth MCP joints: focal thickening, hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed increased flow; mild synovitis in the right second MCP joint.  
- Feet: synovial thickening with hyperemia in the first, second, third, and fifth MTP joints of the right foot and the first and second MTP joints of the left foot.

raw.content:
An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

A 40-year-old man presented with 5 days of progressive dyspnea. On day 1 he was short of breath only with uphill walking (MMRC grade 1), by day 2 he was breathless on level ground (grade 2), and by day 4 he was dyspneic at rest (grade 4). He also noted central, nonradiating chest pain with coughing, without positional change. He denied fever, night sweats, cyanosis, grunting, palpitations, or hemoptysis. He had three previous hospital admissions, most recently 4 months earlier for acute severe pancreatitis. He had a 5-year history of local alcohol consumption but had abstained for 6 months. 

On examination, pulse was 116/min, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, temperature 98 °F, and SpO2 95% on 4 L O2 by nasal prong. He had bilateral pitting edema to the knees. Chest inspection showed decreased movement on the left; trachea deviated rightward; decreased fremitus and stony dullness over the entire left hemithorax; and absent breath sounds on the left. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, WBC 5530/mm3, CRP 73.9 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 145 U/L, serum albumin 3.1 g/dL, serum amylase 486 U/L, and lipase 416 U/L. 

Chest radiograph revealed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with tracheal shift to the right, consistent with massive left pleural effusion. 

Ultrasonography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed a large left pleural effusion with passive basal lung collapse, and showed a normal-sized pancreas with heterogeneous echotexture and a small intrapancreatic collection at the tail. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple non-enhancing cystic areas in the pancreas (largest 23×16 mm in the tail), minimal peripancreatic fat stranding, and no main pancreatic duct dilation or parenchymal calcifications. 

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded 900 mL of dark brown, turbid fluid. Pleural fluid analysis: protein 3.5 g/dL; LDH 1413 U/L; glucose 98 mg/dL; ADA 31.4 U/L; total cell count 100/mm3 (10% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes); amylase 11,871 U/L; PCV 0.8%; no malignant cells; culture negative; MTB/RIF PCR negative.

raw.content:
A 19-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of pain in the plantar aspect of her left foot.  The pain was moderate initially, often worse at night, and markedly exacerbated by compression and exposure to cold.  Over the past four months, the patient noted aggravation of the local pain and was referred for imaging.  She denied any trauma and had no family history of neurofibromatosis.  

On examination, three prominent, soft-tissue nodules with swelling and tenderness were palpated in the plantar aspect of the left foot; they were mobile and not adherent to surrounding tissue.  Sensation testing revealed numbness in the medial distal plantar foot; toe and foot motor strength were normal.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot demonstrated three nodules arranged in a linear distribution in the mid-plantar region.  On T1-weighted images, the lesions were homogeneously isointense to skeletal muscle.  On T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, they were homogeneously hyperintense without cystic degeneration; each was surrounded by a hyperintense rim.  A small extension of high signal from the lateral aspect of one lesion resembled a “mouse-tail.”  Two nodules were located within the flexor digitorum brevis muscle beneath the plantar aponeurosis, and one was in the superficial fascia at the third metatarsophalangeal joint.  The lesions followed the course of branches of the common plantar digital nerves without evidence of invasion.  

Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included glomus tumor, neurofibroma, and schwannoma.  Multiple plexiform schwannoma was suspected, and surgical excision was recommended.

raw.content:
A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, was found on routine blood screening at 10 weeks’ gestation to have pancytopenia: platelet count 85×10^9/L, white-cell count 2.3×10^9/L (neutrophils 1.3×10^9/L, monocytes 0.2×10^9/L), and hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL. She reported occasional easy bruising over the prior two months but no bleeding, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly. Her only prior pregnancy, 13 months earlier, was uncomplicated with normal platelet counts. She had equivocal hypothyroidism, a family history of thyroid disease and systemic lupus erythematosus, and no new medications. Thyroid function, immunoglobulins, folate, and vitamin B12 were normal; antinuclear antibody was negative. Ferritin was low, and iron supplements were started.

She was given a presumptive diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy. Her fatigue persisted but she had no bleeding complications. At 38 weeks’ gestation, with a platelet count of 61×10^9/L, prednisolone 20 mg daily was initiated without response (platelets 65×10^9/L), followed by intravenous immunoglobulin at 1 g/kg (platelets 52×10^9/L). She underwent spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks with minor bleeding; her platelet count was 52×10^9/L, and the neonate’s platelet count was normal.

Five weeks postpartum, she developed a pustular rash on the left upper arm, abdomen, and back. Skin biopsy showed dermal neutrophils with upper dermal edema and a subepidermal blister, consistent with bullous Sweet’s syndrome. Her blood counts remained low: hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, white-cell count 1.7×10^9/L (neutrophils 0.5×10^9/L, monocytes 0.1×10^9/L), and platelets 49×10^9/L.

MR is a male neonate born at 38 weeks’ gestation by elective cesarean delivery. Birth weight was 2350 g (5th–10th percentile), length 45 cm (5th percentile), head circumference 31 cm (<5th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes.  
Maternal history was notable only for immunity to rubella, negative toxoplasma serology, and a single CMV serology at 11 weeks (IgG positive, IgM negative). A maternal febrile episode occurred in the periconceptional period; there was no trauma, and no use of cocaine, warfarin, or anticonvulsants. No family history of bleeding disorders or stroke.  
Fetal ultrasound at 20 weeks suggested intracranial hemorrhage, confirmed by fetal MRI at 25 weeks, which showed a 2.3 cm porencephalic cyst in the right frontotemporal–insular region with ex vacuo enlargement of the right lateral ventricle, reduced right cerebral hemisphere volume, and abnormal micropolygyria of the right frontal cortex.  
At birth, examination revealed microcephaly, jaundice, micropurpura on the face and upper thorax, mild upper limb hypertonicity, and abnormal deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, assays of clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, XIII), protein C and S, von Willebrand factor, alpha-2 antiplasmin, antithrombin, APC resistance, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies, were all normal. Gene sequencing for MTHFR and factor V Leiden was wild type. Newborn metabolic screening was negative.  
Cranial ultrasound on day 1 showed a right porencephalic area with “ex vacuo” enlargement of the right lateral ventricle and a germinolytic cyst on the left; MRI confirmed these findings, with no vascular malformations or thrombosis.

raw.content:
A 53-year-old man was admitted for progressive dyspnea (NYHA class III). His history included a congenital ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood, subsequent aortic valve and septal patch replacements, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic hepatitis C–related liver disease, and prior admission for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. On examination, he had jugular venous distension, irregular rhythm, a 2/6 systolic murmur at the aortic and mitral areas, decreased breath sounds at the right lung base, and peripheral edema.  
ECG showed atrial fibrillation with left bundle branch block. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary congestion and a right basal pleural effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed: a dilated left ventricle with preserved ejection fraction (60%), a dilated right ventricle with normal systolic function, no residual septal shunt, a normally functioning mechanical aortic prosthesis but elevated transprosthetic gradients (mean 33 mmHg) with an effective orifice area index of 0.4 cm2/m2 (suggesting severe prosthesis–patient mismatch), moderate mitral regurgitation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 50 mmHg. The inferior vena cava was dilated with poor inspiratory collapse.  
An initial diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction was made, and intravenous diuretics led to reduction of edema and resolution of radiographic congestion, but the patient remained dyspneic with low exercise tolerance and still required supplemental oxygen.  
A contrast CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed a small right pleural effusion, no lung parenchymal disease or pulmonary embolism, cirrhotic liver with a focal lesion suspicious for hepatocellular carcinoma, splenomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension.  
Right heart catheterization revealed a high cardiac output state, normal pulmonary vascular resistance, and only a slight elevation of mean pulmonary and wedge pressures.

A 10-year-old boy had an 11-month history of changes in most fingernails. Initially, subungual purpuric lesions appeared, followed weeks later by a yellowish discharge from the left thumbnail that was treated with antibiotics for presumed bacterial infection, with only partial improvement. Several months later, he was referred for recurrence and worsening of the lesion. On examination, there was a friable tumor with purulent discharge under the left thumbnail and subungual hemorrhages affecting most fingernails. The scalp showed erythematous, scaly papules with crusts previously diagnosed as seborrheic dermatitis. Biopsies from the nail bed lesion and scalp papules revealed a diffuse infiltrate in the upper dermis of medium-to-large mononuclear cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and reniform nuclei admixed with inflammatory cells. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated positivity for CD1a and S100 protein and negativity for CD68; testing for the BRAF V600E mutation was negative.

A 59-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with one day of left-sided weakness, left facial paresis, difficulty speaking, and drowsiness. His NIH Stroke Scale score on admission was 10. He denied recent head trauma or family history of stroke or thrombosis. He was a non-smoker but used opiates.

Motor testing showed left hemiparesis (3/5 in the arm, 4/5 in the leg) with decreased pain response on the left and an upgoing plantar response on that side.  

An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. A noncontrast head CT performed >24 h after symptom onset revealed an acute right MCA territory infarct in the right parietotemporal lobe. Twenty-four hours later, because of worsening consciousness, a repeat CT showed a new infarct in the left frontal lobe (left MCA territory).  

Initial laboratory results included a platelet count of 77 × 10^3/μL and hemoglobin 15 g/dL. Over the next several days, the platelet count declined to 21 × 10^3/μL, and hemoglobin fell to 11.8 g/dL. Reticulocytes were 2.6%, LDH was 1148 U/L, total bilirubin rose from 1.9 mg/dL to 4.4 mg/dL (indirect bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL), and acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, D-dimer) were elevated. Coagulation studies, troponin, liver function tests, lipid profile, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear showed occasional schistocytes. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative.

raw.content:
An 80-year-old woman with a history of rectal cancer treated in 2008 by liver metastasectomy followed by Hartmann’s procedure with intraoperative radiotherapy (5×5 Gy) and adjuvant capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab presented in January 2011 with intermittent gross hematuria. Since December 2009 she had bilateral JJ stents for ureteral strictures, replaced regularly. In November 2010 she required drainage of a pelvic abscess after stent occlusion complicated by Candida glabrata infection. Her medical history also included type 2 diabetes mellitus and angina pectoris.

On presentation, her hemoglobin was 7.2 mmol/L and creatinine was 370 μmol/L. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis. Because of persistent hematuria and suspected stent occlusion, cystoscopy and ureteral stent exchange were performed: removal of the right double-J catheter revealed pulsatile arterial bleeding from the right ureteral orifice. The stent was changed, bleeding subsided, and she received four units of packed red cells intraoperatively. Open surgery was considered too high risk.

A CT angiogram demonstrated active hemorrhage at the right renal pelvis with clots in the collecting system. The patient was hemodynamically stable and managed expectantly, but that night she had recurrent gross hematuria. Embolisation of the right renal artery with coils was performed. During subsequent left stent repositioning, retrograde ureterography revealed a ureteroileal fistula, and a new ureteral catheter was placed; conservative management was advised. Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 80-year-old woman was referred for management of a chronic superficial sacral wound present for approximately 2 years. She reported progressively worsening sacral pain and local skin irritation but denied purulent discharge, altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or rectal discharge. Her history was notable for inverse psoriasis affecting the natal cleft, prior coccygectomy 20 years earlier, multiple cutaneous nonmelanoma skin cancers, ischemic heart disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, hypertension, dyslipidemia, mild asthma, and splenectomy. Medications included aspirin, rosuvastatin, valsartan, and topical corticosteroids as needed.

On examination, she was afebrile and systemically well. The coccygectomy scar was slightly indurated and surrounded by a broad area of excoriated skin with plaques and focal ulceration in the upper natal cleft. A small superior sinus tract without obvious pits and mild serous discharge were noted. The lesion was located more than 5 cm from the anal verge. There was no exophytic mass, no underlying abscess cavity, and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast demonstrated a 6 × 13 × 28 mm area of nonspecific, irregular superficial enhancement in the natal cleft without invasion of underlying structures, no visible sinus tract, and no regional nodal or bony metastases. A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 1-year-old girl was brought with sudden onset of hematemesis; the vomitus resembled coffee grounds. She was born full-term, had no significant medical or family history, no allergies, and no medication use, including NSAIDs. On arrival she was lethargic; temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 160 bpm, respiratory rate 24 bpm, blood pressure 83/35 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on 2 L nasal oxygen. Physical examination showed pallor but was otherwise unremarkable. A nasogastric tube aspirated a small amount of blood. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 9,500/μL; hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL; platelets 220×10^3/μL; CRP 0.55 mg/dL; normal liver function tests; prothrombin time 13.2 s (INR 1.01); aPTT 31.7 s; normal factor XIII and plasma gastrin levels; ESR 2 mm/h. Serologies for cytomegalovirus-IgM, EBV-VCA-IgM, and H. pylori-IgG were negative, and stool antigen testing excluded H. pylori. Blood cultures and stool parasite testing were negative. Abdominal radiography and ultrasonography were normal, and contrast-enhanced CT showed no active bleeding. She received two units of packed red blood cells and famotidine, yet her hemoglobin remained low. Thus, on hospital day 2, early upper endoscopy was planned to identify the bleeding source.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 62-year-old man was admitted on June 25, 2021, with a 20-day history of episodic slurred speech that had worsened over the previous 9 days. Initially, episodes lasted about 10 minutes without loss of consciousness, headache, dizziness, diplopia, dysphagia, or limb weakness; by presentation, they occurred 2–3 times daily lasting about 30 minutes. His medical history included hypertension (>20 years), diabetes mellitus (8 years), and coronary heart disease (8 years); he was blind bilaterally after retinal detachment in adolescence. He denied smoking and alcohol use. On examination, temperature was 36.5°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 17/min, and blood pressure 144/86 mmHg. Cranial nerve exam showed dysarthria and midline tongue extension; limb strength was 5/5 with normal tone; Babinski and other reflexes were normal; he had no light perception with irregular pupils and absent light reflexes. Routine blood tests, coagulation studies, rheumatologic panels, thyroid function, tumor markers, liver and kidney function, and electrolytes were all normal. Brain MRI and susceptibility-weighted imaging were unremarkable; MRA showed mild cerebral arteriosclerosis; carotid MRA showed carotid arteriosclerosis with limited stenosis of the intracranial left vertebral artery; transcranial Doppler was normal. The initial diagnosis was transient ischemic attack of the vertebrobasilar system. On review, symptoms did not improve with rest; a fatigue test and a neostigmine test were both negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 65-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and bronchial asthma presented with mild headaches of several months’ duration and no focal neurologic deficits. He had undergone cranial MRI 4 years earlier for unrelated reasons, with no significant change in the identified lesion since then. Laboratory studies were normal. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a well-defined, 19-mm mass in the left parietal bone near the squamosal suture, centred in the diploic space, with sparse but preserved trabeculae and a slight bony bulge, without disruption of the inner or outer tables. MRI showed the lesion to be isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images, with multiple internal hyperintense foci, heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images, and restricted diffusion. The hyperintense foci on T1 images were presumed to represent bone marrow fat, and the preserved trabecular architecture suggested that pre-existing structures were not destroyed.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
