A 4-year-old girl of Turkish ancestry was brought to the emergency department for progressive unsteadiness and recurrent falls over the preceding 5 days. Five days earlier she had first noted staggering and grabbing for support to avoid falls; during her initial fall she sustained a nasal bridge laceration that required suturing. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
 Three-month history of “ear problems” was elicited: initial diagnosis of otitis media with effusion and tympanic perforation treated with antibiotics led to partial resolution. On current otoscopic examination, the left tympanic membrane was intact without effusion; the right external canal was occluded by polypoid tissue and purulent secretion. A Frenzel’s examination showed no nystagmus.  
 Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and temporal bones revealed bilateral osteolysis of the mastoids, superior and lateral semicircular canals, and the right external auditory canal, plus a separate osteolytic lesion in the dorsal left parietal bone. There was also adenoid hypertrophy and mild sinus mucosal thickening.  
 Brainstem evoked response audiometry demonstrated a threshold of 40 dB with normal wave latencies on the left and an 80 dB threshold with prolonged wave I latency on the right, indicating profound right-sided hearing loss.

raw.content:
An 86-year-old woman with a history of dementia, living in a non–air-conditioned room during a heat wave, was found unconscious and brought to the emergency department. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 6 (E1V1M4), body temperature 42.4 °C, blood pressure 88/40 mm Hg, and pulse rate 120 beats/min. Laboratory studies revealed hepatic dysfunction, renal dysfunction, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Head MRI and MRA showed no abnormality. She was diagnosed with severe heat stroke (APACHE II score 42, SOFA score 15), intubated, and treated with extracorporeal cooling, fluid resuscitation, and DIC therapy; fursultiamine and levothyroxine were also given. Despite treatment, she remained unconscious. On day 6, brain MRI showed bilateral cerebellar hemisphere high-signal intensity on diffusion-weighted and FLAIR images with corresponding low ADC signals. On day 9, SPECT with 123I-IMP demonstrated decreased perfusion in the right cerebellar hemisphere. By day 13, MRI abnormalities had begun to improve, and her level of consciousness improved to E4VTM6.

raw.content:
An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

raw.content:
A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

raw.content:
A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history presented in December with a 4-day history of fever to 38.8 °C, shaking chills, hemoptysis, and worsening dyspnea. He reported several months of intermittent night sweats, arthralgias of the wrists and ankles, and a 10-kg weight loss. One day before admission, he noted a painful ecchymotic lesion on his left calf; over the next 24 hours, similar lesions appeared on his abdomen, back, right upper arm, and right calf. His 3-year-old son had recently had a respiratory illness. On examination, temperature was 35.3 °C, blood pressure 117/75 mmHg, pulse 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 29 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Bilateral wheezes were present, and there were multiple painful ecchymoses with hemorrhagic bullae over the trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 9000/mm3 (87% neutrophils), hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, normal renal and liver function, lactate dehydrogenase 799 IU/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 81 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 38.5 mg/dL. Chest radiography and CT demonstrated multifocal alveolar infiltrates, and CT angiography showed no pulmonary embolism. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin were started for presumed community-acquired pneumonia. On hospital day 2, a punch biopsy of a skin lesion revealed superficial and deep dermal thrombotic paucicellular vasculopathy involving skin appendages without significant neutrophils or leukocytoclasia. Tests for cryoglobulin, protein C, protein S, rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, complement levels, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:160; lupus anticoagulant was prolonged at 82 seconds (reference range, 27–41); anticardiolipin IgM was 64 (reference range, 0–12); and anti–phosphatidylserine IgM was >100 (reference range, <10). Nasopharyngeal testing for influenza antigen, streptococcal antigen, and Legionella antigen was negative. A FilmArray respiratory panel was positive for respiratory syncytial virus and negative for other respiratory viruses and atypical bacteria. Epstein-Barr virus DNA PCR was positive at 8696 copies/mL; tests for HIV, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis A, B, and C were negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 17-year-old nulliparous female presented with a two-year history of gradually progressive abdominal distension. She initially sought evaluation for bloating but was advised to diet for presumed weight gain. She denied pain, vaginal bleeding, or systemic symptoms. There was no personal or family history of cancer. On examination, her BMI was 20.5 kg/m2, blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, pulse 89/min, and SpO2 95% on room air. The abdomen was markedly distended with a palpable mass rising approximately 3 cm above the umbilicus. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an 18 cm diameter ovarian tumor. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL with a microcytic profile (MCV 73.2 fL); APTT, INR, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine were normal. Tumor markers included HE4 69.1 pmol/L (N ≤ 60.5), LDH 202 U/L (N ≤ 48.5), with alpha-fetoprotein 4.54 ng/mL (N ≤ 5.8), CA-125 23.1 U/mL (N ≤ 35), and β-hCG <0.2 mIU/mL all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, fluid-filled lesion measuring 19.3 × 6.2 × 21 cm, located in the pelvis and mid-abdomen, displacing the uterus and compressing the aorta and inferior vena cava. The lesion appeared unilocular with a 1.5 mm wall and no septations or solid components, and was suggestive of an ovarian origin.

Laboratory studies showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 220 U/L (reference range, 30–95), a phosphorus level of 2.1 mg/dL (2.5–5.0), creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, and 25-OH vitamin D 14.8 ng/mL (30–95). Bone densitometry showed Z-scores of −2.5 in the lumbar spine and −1.9 in the femoral neck, and an octreotide scan was negative. She was treated with calcitriol and phosphate and underwent percutaneous pinning of the femoral neck. She became pregnant; her phosphate and calcitriol were adjusted to maintain normal phosphorus levels, and genetic evaluation for hypophosphatemic disorders, including X-linked hypophosphatemia, was unremarkable. Family history was negative for bone disease. After a planned cesarean delivery, she continued to have disabling bilateral hip, knee, and ankle pain. On re-presentation, examination revealed a slow gait with a limp and lumbar tenderness. Current labs on calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and elemental phosphorus 500 mg twice daily included alkaline phosphatase 204 U/L, phosphorus 1.6 mg/dL, 25-OH vitamin D 32 ng/mL, 1,25[OH]2D3 32.4 pg/mL, calcium 9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and parathyroid hormone 74 pg/mL. Phosphate supplementation was increased to three times daily, raising the phosphorus level to 2.3 mg/dL. A gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/MRI showed a 9×8-mm intracortical lesion in the anterolateral right fibular head (standard uptake value [SUV], 65), with additional uptake in a right femoral neck stress fracture (SUV, 5.6) and bilateral calcaneal stress fractures (SUV, 4).

raw.content:
A 57-year-old man with stage cS4a mantle cell lymphoma in complete remission after induction chemoimmunotherapy presented in August 2018 with painful swelling of the calves. There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. Diuretics gave transient relief, but over weeks the swelling spread to the upper extremities and trunk muscles. Systemic steroids and a short discontinuation of ibrutinib had no effect.

By November 2018, calf swelling worsened; examination was notable only for one slightly enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Laboratory tests showed elevated LDH and CK, with negative autoimmune serology. Analgesics provided minimal benefit. In January 2019, CT scan showed no lymphoma relapse but diffuse subcutaneous edema. The patient’s condition deteriorated, and he was hospitalized with generalized muscle pain, ECOG performance status 3, massive edema (especially of the lower extremities), and extreme muscle tenderness. Neurologic exam showed only weak symmetric fist closure and shoulder lift; no focal deficits.

Initial evaluations were consistent with myositis of unknown cause. Ibrutinib and rituximab were discontinued. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, transaminases, CK, troponin I, myoglobin, and LDH, with reduced plasma protein, albumin, and IgG; leukocyte count was elevated. MRI of the thighs showed diffuse intramuscular and extramuscular edema. Muscle biopsy demonstrated interstitial and perivascular T-cell and macrophage infiltrates with variation in fiber size, centrally located nuclei, necrosis, and regeneration. The patient developed acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Troponin I rose further; ECG revealed a new right bundle branch block and repolarization disturbances, and he developed atrial fibrillation. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocarditis. Over the next days, increasing somnolence and personality changes were noted. Brain MRI was unremarkable, but spinal MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion concerning for myelitis. CSF analysis showed leukocyte count 329/μl, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, and protein 79.6 mg/dl.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 64-year-old woman presented with a slowly enlarging mass in the left labia majora over 10 years. Her vital signs were normal. On examination, the mass was firm, painless, immobile, and measured approximately 7 × 4 cm, extending toward the mons pubis. Routine laboratory tests were normal. 

Surgical history:
– In 2000, a mass in the Bartholin’s gland was excised; histopathology in 2007 showed chondroid syringoma.  
– One year later, a recurrence in the labia majora was resected; histology showed clear cell hidradenoma (“lobular glandular proliferation of cuboid cells with no anaplasia”).  
– Most recently, ultrasound revealed a 4.2 × 8 cm heterogeneous, hypervascular subcutaneous mass; CT scan demonstrated a 3.8 × 7.2 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing lesion in the left labia majora extending to the anterior perineum, and a low-density focus in the liver suggestive of a simple cyst.  
– The vulvar mass was excised; on gross examination it measured 7 × 3 × 4 cm, was gray and well-circumscribed, and was reported again as chondroid syringoma.  

Three months later, the patient noted another recurrence near the fourchette. The lesion was excised and submitted for histopathologic evaluation.

A previously healthy young man presented during a month of religious fasting with a 1-week history of intractable vomiting, postprandial upper abdominal pain, and bloating. He had been compliant with fasting customs, was markedly lean, and reported progressive inability to tolerate oral intake. On examination, he was dehydrated and exhausted. After initial resuscitation, abdominal ultrasonography and plain radiographs showed marked gastric distension. A nasogastric tube was placed for decompression. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta at an acute angle. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal, with no intrinsic luminal lesions.

raw.content:
A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

raw.content:
A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

A 48‐year‐old woman with a history of asthma presented with a 2‐day history of right lower‐extremity numbness and pain that worsened despite conservative measures. She denied any low back pain. On examination, manual muscle testing of the right tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus was 3/5, and gastrocnemius and flexor hallucis longus were 4/5; deep‐tendon reflexes were normal. Straight‐leg‐raising was positive at 70 degrees; the femoral‐nerve stretch test was negative. 

Plain radiographs showed degenerative scoliosis at L5–S1. Lumbar MRI demonstrated a right‐sided disc herniation at L5–S1 without significant nerve‐root or cord compression. Initial peroneal‐nerve conduction studies revealed a motor conduction velocity of 51.5 m/s. Ankle‐brachial indices were decreased (0.78 on the right, 0.73 on the left), but lower‐extremity arteriography showed no significant vascular lesions. Based on these findings, she was diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation and treated symptomatically with Neurotropin®. 

By day 7, muscle strength nearly normalized, but lateral leg pain persisted. On day 22, pain increased, and by day 26 she developed right foot drop (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, flexor hallucis longus, and peroneus longus 1/5; left side 4/5) with absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally. Urgent MRI showed no new nerve‐root compression. Repeat peroneal conduction studies failed to elicit an evoked myogenic potential. On day 30, she was unable to walk and was admitted for further evaluation.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 1.5-year history of abdominal pain and three loose, watery stools daily. He had gastroesophageal reflux disease and hereditary hemochromatosis (grade 3 iron overload, mild portal fibrosis, C282Y homozygosity). He denied rectal bleeding, fever, or weight loss. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination was unremarkable. 
 
Laboratory evaluation showed negative ova and parasites, bacterial culture, fecal leukocytes, and Clostridium difficile NAAT. Histoplasma antigen, anti-transglutaminase, and anti-endomysial antibodies were negative. Rapid plasma reagin and Tropheryma whipplei testing were also negative. 
 
Colonoscopy revealed erythematous mucosa in the transverse colon and rectum and congestion in the terminal ileum. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed diffuse gastric erythema with erosions and duodenitis. Biopsies from the stomach, duodenum, terminal ileum, colon, and rectum all demonstrated non-caseating microgranulomas; acid-fast bacilli and fungal stains were negative, and no Helicobacter pylori organisms were identified. 
 
CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed hepatosplenomegaly; a prior liver biopsy showed no granulomas. Chest CT was unremarkable. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level was elevated at 77 U/L.

A 40-year-old previously healthy man was admitted after 1 week of progressive apathy, unresponsiveness, and immobility. He became bedridden and required a feeding tube and urinary catheter. On transfer, he was in a vegetative state.  
Vital signs: temperature 36.5 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 135/78 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E3 V1 M3). Pupils 3.5 mm, briskly reactive; corneal reflexes present. Both axial and appendicular muscles were rigid, with flexed arms and extended legs; bilateral Babinski and Chaddock signs were positive.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 3.79×10^9/L, neutrophils 74%, CRP 6.07 mg/L, ESR 21 mm/h; HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ANA, anticardiolipin, ANCA, and T-spot negative. Liver and renal functions were normal.  
Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 50 mmH₂O; CSF clear, protein 3.64 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L (blood glucose 5.38 mmol/L), chloride 123 mmol/L, leukocytes 0/mm³. CSF India ink stain and bacterial cultures were negative. CSF oligoclonal bands, AQP4, MOG, and GFAP antibodies were negative; CSF fungal cultures were negative.  
Imaging: Brain CT showed a hypodense lesion in the corpus callosum. MRI revealed a homogeneous mass in the corpus callosum body, hypointense on T1, isointense on T2 FLAIR, with rim enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema on postcontrast T1. DWI demonstrated rim hyperintensity but no central restricted diffusion.

A 36-year-old woman presented with persistent severe pain on the left side of her face. Two months earlier, on the day after receiving her third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, she experienced episodic sharp, electric-shock–like pain initially affecting the entire left hemiface. Attacks lasted 4–5 seconds, were triggered by jaw movement during eating or tooth brushing, and reached 10/10 on a numeric pain scale. She reported allodynia to cold air and hypersensitivity to touch in the affected area. During attacks, she described distorted sensations in the V2 region, but sensory testing was otherwise normal. She had no other neurological deficits, no relevant past medical or family history, and prior doses of the same vaccine had been uneventful. Routine laboratory tests, including D-dimer, were normal. RT-qPCR for SARS-CoV-2 and other infections was negative. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head showed no abnormalities.

raw.content:
An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal.  
Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury.  
An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.  
Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

A 60-year-old man with a history of heavy cigarette smoking, emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission presented with a 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding, innumerable hepatic nodules, mural thickening of the cecum and sigmoid colon, and marked mesenteric, para-aortic, and portocaval lymphadenopathy; there was also pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a perforated appendix with four-quadrant purulent contamination and a thickened, woody sigmoid colon; a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy was performed. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability was brought to the hospital after a witnessed collapse. She had no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease, and her family denied any illicit drug or alcohol use. While at a noisy auto mechanic shop, she became pale and lost consciousness; bystander ECG showed ventricular fibrillation. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after two defibrillations. On arrival, her blood pressure was 93/70 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, and oxygen saturation 100% (bag–valve–mask). An intravenous amiodarone infusion (1 mg/min) and oral amiodarone 400 mg were administered. On examination she was comatose (GCS 3), with agonal respirations; cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. In the intensive care unit, her differential diagnosis included channelopathies, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and metabolic abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed normal chemistry panel and electrolytes. Initial electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm with interpolated premature ventricular complexes and a QTc of 380 ms, without any evidence of infarction, pre-excitation, or Brugada pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 45–50%, normal wall thickness, and no valvular abnormalities.

A 35-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of radicular pain radiating from her lower back down the left leg, with occasional tingling. The pain progressively worsened and was particularly severe by August. She denied any weakness, autonomic symptoms, history of trauma, or injury. On examination, she had mild hypesthesia in the left L5–S1 dermatome but normal muscle strength, normal abduction and adduction, and negative Lasègue, Kernig, Bragard, and Sicard signs. Electromyography showed neuropathic irritation of the left L4, L5, S1, and S2 roots, most severe at L5, with no denervation. Lumbosacral gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed a solitary, completely cystic mass in the left L5–S1 foraminal zone extending along the course of the sciatic nerve into the left ischial groove, measuring approximately 13.9 cm in length and 1.9 cm in maximal diameter. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement, causing severe foraminal stenosis without attachment to pelvic organs. MR neurography confirmed that the mass arose from the sciatic nerve at the left ischial groove.

raw.content:
A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. She initially noted difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair; over weeks she became wheelchair-bound. She also reported morning stiffness of both small hand joints lasting about 30 minutes, dysphagia for solids and liquids, and poor appetite, without fever or weight loss.

Her medical history was notable for thyroiditis in 2015 that resolved without long-term therapy. Family history included a younger sister with Prader–Willi syndrome. She was up to date on vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic testing showed symmetric muscle strength of 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, with brisk reflexes more pronounced on the left. She could not stand from the wheelchair unaided. In the left hand, she was unable to make a fist or tuck the fingers; there was tenderness at the fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 2.96 × 10^3/µL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.8 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (109.2 mm/hr), and normal creatine kinase (39 U/L). Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH (0.017 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (20.9 pmol/L), normal free T3 (4.53 pmol/L), and markedly elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (3410 IU/mL). Antinuclear antibody titer was 27 (reference <20); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA were negative. Viral serologies, renal and liver tests, and other hormonal assays were normal.

Hyperkalemic paralysis was ruled out. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goiter consistent with thyroiditis. MRI of the brain and lumbosacral spine was normal; cervical spine MRI showed a small C6–C7 disc herniation. Incidentally, the lumbosacral spine MRI revealed bilateral sacroiliitis. Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. Although myositis was suspected, electromyography and repeat creatine kinase were normal.

raw.content:
A 34‐year‐old African American man with hemophilia A, HIV‐1 infection, and hepatitis C virus infection presented with a 3‐month history of intermittent fever, unintentional weight loss, and progressive lip swelling with painful ulcerations. Six months earlier he had resumed antiretroviral therapy, with his CD4 count rising from 94 to 160 cells/mm3; the lip lesions developed approximately two months after the CD4 count began to improve. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids without benefit. He was taking acyclovir for herpes simplex prophylaxis and dapsone for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. 

On examination, his lips were markedly edematous, with multiple superficial ulcers having heaped‐up margins. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. The initial differential diagnosis included herpetic ulcers, bacterial infection, fungal infection, and angioedema. 

Diagnostic studies showed an undetectable HIV viral load and undetectable hepatitis C viral load. A polymerase‐chain‐reaction assay for herpes simplex virus from an ulcer base was negative. Complement C1 esterase inhibitor levels were within normal limits. Gram stain, acid‐fast stain, and mucicarmine stain of lesion samples were negative. Fungal blood cultures and both urine and serum Histoplasma antigen tests were negative.

raw.content:
A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. 

She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. 

Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Because of the absence of pathological enhancement of the pons, this was felt to represent either an aggressive demyelinating process or a low-grade glioma. The patient continued to deteriorate, became comatose, and died approximately four weeks after admission.

raw.content:
A 67‐year‐old man with a 3‐year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, glimepiride, and a prior percutaneous coronary intervention for acute myocardial infarction 2 months earlier was referred for treatment of newly diagnosed extensive ulcerative colitis. He had a 40‐year smoking history but had quit after his myocardial infarction. He reported four episodes of bloody diarrhea daily but denied abdominal pain or fever. On admission for a 2‐week educational trial of a plant‐based diet, his body weight was 69 kg and physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed normal white‐cell count, bilirubin, and liver function tests. Ten days after admission, plasma glucose rose from 258 mg/dL to 449 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c increased from 7.3% to 8.0%. Urinalysis showed no proteinuria but microalbuminuria of 50.7 mg/day. Anti–glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies were negative. Both serum amylase and lipase were elevated. Contrast‐enhanced CT and MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrated swelling of the pancreas with a peripheral rim and slight narrowing of the main pancreatic duct. Serum IgG4 was 36.0 mg/dL (reference range, 4.5–117 mg/dL).

A 53-year-old Hispanic man with no prior comorbidities presented with a two-week history of recurrent cough, nonmassive hemoptysis, and central chest pain. One month earlier, he had mild COVID-19 not requiring hospitalization. He also reported fatigue, myalgias, and anorexia but denied fever, dyspnea, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, he was tachycardic but in no acute distress; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (25.56×10^3/μL), blood urea nitrogen 107 mg/dL, creatinine 5.8 mg/dL (baseline unknown), mild transaminitis, hyponatremia, and hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis and urine indices were ordered.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral scattered infiltrates with a denser consolidation in the right upper lobe. Noncontrast chest CT revealed multiple peripheral patchy consolidations in both lungs, some cavitating. These findings were interpreted as multifocal pneumonia.

He received intravenous azithromycin and ceftriaxone, intravenous bicarbonate, and emergent hemodialysis for acute kidney injury. Blood, sputum, and urine cultures were obtained, and PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.

raw.content:
A 54-year-old fisherman with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department after a rapid ascent from a 50 m sea‐depth saturation dive. He complained of dyspnea, lethargy, severe generalized arthralgia, and mild confusion. He was alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. Physical examination showed bilateral joint pain worsened by movement without erythema or swelling; neurological, chest, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Vital signs were blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 95 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, and temperature 36.6 °C. The Wells pulmonary embolism score was 3.

High‐flow oxygen was started. An electrocardiogram was normal. Posterior–anterior chest radiography showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 13 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 73 mg/L, and otherwise normal hemoglobin, platelets, glucose, ESR, creatinine, urea, potassium, sodium, and D-dimer. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated metabolic acidosis with pH 7.32, PCO2 28 mm Hg, HCO3– 15 mmol/L, and PO2 63 mm Hg. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal biventricular size and function and no valvular disease; however, spontaneous echo contrast consistent with microbubbles was seen in the right heart chambers. A Valsalva maneuver–enhanced color‐flow Doppler study showed no evidence of a patent foramen ovale.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, chills, or fever. She had no history of hepatitis, surgery, or hereditary disease, and no underlying medical conditions. On examination, she was afebrile and oriented; there was right upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or palpable masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, and negative Murphy’s sign and shifting dullness.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• AFP 2.4 µg/l (normal 0.0–7.0)  
• CEA 11.6 µg/l (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• CA-125 32.3 KIU/l (normal 0.0–35.0)  
• CA19-9 228.0 KIU/l (normal 0.0–30.0)  
• Other liver enzymes and blood counts largely within reference ranges, except WBC 11.9×10^9/l (normal 3.5–9.5×10^9/l).

Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous echoic mass near the gallbladder fossa in the right liver lobe, calcifications in the right liver, multiple gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, and enhanced pancreatic echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lesion in the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the gallbladder fossa, multiple enlarged hepatic hilar lymph nodes, and findings of gallstones with cholecystitis. Liver MRI demonstrated an occupying lesion in the right lobe with mild intrahepatic bile duct dilatation, raising the possibility of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, along with gallstones and cholecystitis. No extrahepatic primary tumor was identified.

A 38-year-old woman presented with 4 months of progressively worsening symmetric pain in the small joints of her hands, wrists, knees, and ankles. She reported early morning stiffness lasting 2 hours daily and severe fatigue throughout the day. One month before presentation, she had a mild COVID-19 infection confirmed by SARS-CoV-2 PCR; symptoms were limited to fever, chills, and a non-oxygen-requiring cough. She had not been vaccinated against COVID-19 at that time. She denied fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, rash, or appetite changes since recovering. There were no recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections and no history of psoriasis or uveitis. She is a non-smoker, does not drink alcohol, and has no recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a maternal aunt with rheumatoid arthritis.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 13 mm/hour and a C-reactive protein of 4.3 mg/L (both within normal limits). Immunologic testing revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, negative extractable nuclear antigen and double-stranded DNA antibodies, a rheumatoid factor of 62.29 IU/mL (normal <20 IU/mL), and an anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody of 237.39 units (normal <20 units). Hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Radiographs of the hands, knees, ankles, and feet were unremarkable. Hand ultrasound showed no joint erosion. MRI of the hands demonstrated synovitis of the bilateral distal radioulnar joints and the left second metacarpophalangeal joint, with tenosynovitis around the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon; no osseous destruction was identified.

raw.content:
A 37-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjögren’s syndrome was diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis and scheduled for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy before starting prednisolone. She had never received acid-secretion inhibitors, including proton pump inhibitors or vonoprazan. Vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. 

Endoscopic findings:
- Antrum: normal appearance.
- Gastric corpus: normal coloration with a regular arrangement of collecting venules; red streaks and slight mucosal swelling on the lesser curvature of the angle.
- Magnified narrow-band imaging of the corpus: regular round pit patterns.

Biopsy sites: greater curvature of the prepyloric area and lesser and greater curvatures of the gastric corpus.

Histologic findings (lesser curvature of corpus):
- Three defined layers: first (foveolar epithelium) showed foveolar hyperplasia; second (parietal cells) was shortened with mild degeneration; third (chief cells) preserved.
- Layer contours slightly disorganized with mild lymphocytic infiltration.
- H+/K+-ATPase staining: heterogeneously reduced.
- Pepsinogen I: uneven staining.
- MUC6: positive throughout the region.
- Chromogranin A: slight enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia.

Laboratory tests after endoscopy:
- Anti-parietal cell antibody: <1:10 (negative)
- Anti-intrinsic factor antibody: negative
- Serum gastrin: 150 pg/mL (normal 37–172)
- Vitamin B12: 870 pg/mL (normal 233–914)
- Anti-H. pylori IgG: <3 U/mL (negative)

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 38-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of hypertension first noted at age 24 during pregnancy and again at age 38 after a basal ganglia hemorrhage. She had been diagnosed with splenomegaly of unknown cause at age 21; her younger brother had a similar finding. During her admission for hemorrhage, she underwent a decompressive craniectomy and was noted to have:  
- Normochromic microcytic anemia and thrombocytopenia on full blood examination; other laboratory tests, including thyroid function, cortisol, aldosterone–renin ratio, urinary metanephrines, and renal function, were unremarkable.  
- Lipid profile showed low HDL and elevated triglycerides.  
- Renal Doppler ultrasound excluded renal artery stenosis but revealed incidental bilateral adrenal lesions and hepatosplenomegaly.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed bilateral adrenal lesions (32 HU noncontrast; absolute washout 76.5%, relative washout 39%) that were unchanged after 8 months, and gross hepatosplenomegaly with dilated portal and splenic veins.  
She had no symptoms of adrenal hormone excess, and her blood pressure was controlled on a single antihypertensive agent.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A male newborn was referred at 1 day of age for cyanosis; oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 80% in room air. Laboratory findings showed a hematocrit of 47.8% and a platelet count of 103 000/mm3; other values were normal and there were no signs of infection. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus. A prostaglandin infusion was started, raising SaO2 to 90–95%. On day 11, he underwent a systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunt operation with graft placement and PDA division. Preoperative values on day 10 were hematocrit 38.9%, platelet count 173 000/mm3, and SaO2 95% on prostaglandin. Postoperatively, hematocrit was 52.1% and platelet count was 58 000/mm3; platelet count then increased without transfusion. By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. He was discharged on postoperative day 13 with SaO2 85–87%, hematocrit 33.4%, and platelet count 225 000/mm3.

At 10 months of age, he was admitted for a Rastelli operation. His SaO2 was 80%; hematocrit was 49.1% and platelet count was 68 000/mm3. He had no bleeding history or medications. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and INR were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Antiplatelet antibodies and platelet‐associated immunoglobulins were negative; antinuclear and anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies were normal. Platelet aggregation time was 127 s (reference, 61–110 s). Viral and bacterial studies were insignificant. The pediatrician made a provisional diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia and administered intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg) the day before surgery. On the day of operation, hematocrit was 42.6% and platelet count was 77 000/mm3.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 17-year-old single Turkish woman presented with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, and right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. She had no known exposure to tuberculosis. On examination she was afebrile with tender right lower abdominal quadrant and no rebound. Initial abdominal and chest radiographs were normal, and a bedside abdominal ultrasound showed no abnormalities. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,200/μL, C-reactive protein of 12 mg/L, blood urea nitrogen of 35 mg/dL, and creatinine of 1.02 mg/dL. Urinalysis was unremarkable and a urine human chorionic gonadotropin test was negative. HIV testing was negative. While under observation, a second abdominopelvic ultrasound was interpreted as suggestive of retrocecal appendicitis. The patient was taken to the operating room via a McBurney’s incision. A 15 × 6 cm cystic mass with regular margins was found arising from the right tubo-ovarian complex; the appendix appeared clinically normal. The mass was excised intact, the tubo-ovarian structures were preserved, and on incision of the cyst wall purulent fluid was noted. Cultures were deferred until after the weekend.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes presented with several days of urinary retention and inability to ambulate in the setting of a 1-year history of progressive lower-extremity weakness and a 100-lb unintentional weight loss. Her weakness began in the proximal left leg, gradually involved the right leg and both hands, and was accompanied by worsening numbness and tingling in her feet; she became wheelchair-dependent within 6 months. She denied pain, flank pain, hematuria, fevers, visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulty. On examination, she was alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II–XII were intact. She had bilateral weakness of hip flexors, knee flexors, knee extensors, and intrinsic hand muscles, with atrophy of the hands and thighs. Sensation to light touch was reduced in the feet, with slight impairment of vibration and proprioception. Reflexes were 2+ in the upper extremities and absent at the knees and ankles; plantar responses were flexor. Bladder catheterization yielded 1.8 L of retained urine. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; sodium 117 mmol/L; chloride 87 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen 0.89 mg/dL; creatinine 25 mg/dL. Urine was negative for protein or bacteria. CSF analysis revealed protein 175 mg/dL, glucose 105 mg/dL, 1 WBC, 0 RBC; CSF cytology was negative for malignancy. Lyme serology, autoimmune panel, and a comprehensive paraneoplastic antibody panel were negative. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.5 g/dL. On hospital day 4, electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated decreased amplitudes in motor and sensory nerves, slowed conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, and absent sensory responses, suggesting a chronic length-dependent sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy with superimposed chronic lumbosacral plexopathy. MRI of the pelvis showed bilateral femoral nerve enlargement without enhancement.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 27-year-old man with a history of a 5 mm‐thick melanoma on his posterior neck treated six years earlier by wide local excision (no sentinel lymph node biopsy, no adjuvant therapy) presented with hemoptysis and dyspnea. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for scattered breath sounds without stridor. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 3.1 × 2.7 × 3.6 cm mass in the right lower lobe. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the lung lesion demonstrated a malignant small round blue cell tumor. Molecular studies were negative for an EWSR1 translocation but otherwise were interpreted as consistent with Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET). 

Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT showed an FDG-avid right lower lobe mass and an intensely FDG-avid, partially calcified 4.1 × 2.3 × 2.8 cm expansile lesion within the right hyoid bone. Ultrasound–guided core needle biopsy of the hyoid lesion was nondiagnostic, yielding only rare atypical epithelial cells amidst lymphocytes.

A multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor board concluded that the hyoid lesion most likely represented a synchronous primary bone tumor (e.g., plasmacytoma, chondrosarcoma, or osteosarcoma). Given his pulmonary symptoms and the potential for chemotherapy to treat both lesions, he received 14 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide (VCD/IE). 

Mid-treatment PET/CT demonstrated a substantial decrease in size and complete metabolic response of the lung mass but development of right neck adenopathy and interval growth of the hyoid bone lesion, suggesting a distinct pathology.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 54-year-old man with glioblastoma treated by surgical resection began a clinical trial with M7824 (a bifunctional fusion protein targeting PD-L1 and TGF-β). Four weeks after initiation of M7824, he presented with a severely pruritic, nontender, erythematous papular and macular eruption on his back, bilateral ankles, and upper extremities. He was not receiving any other new medications. The oncology team initially classified the eruption as a grade I rash and prescribed hydrocortisone 1% cream and oral diphenhydramine, but the rash and pruritus progressed. One month later, the rash reached grade II severity, and doxycycline was started for a suspected acneiform eruption. On dermatologic evaluation, the consensus was that the eruption represented a drug reaction to M7824. Laboratory evaluation showed no elevations in liver enzymes, no eosinophilia, and no lymphadenopathy. The patient was treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment and hydroxyzine, but over the following two weeks the rash progressed to grade III with worsening pruritus. M7824 infusions were held, and prednisone at 40 mg per day was initiated according to guidelines, but his symptoms failed to improve.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 6‐year‐old girl with no relevant medical history presented with intensely pruritic skin lesions on her anterior thighs. The lesions first appeared 2 weeks earlier in recurrent 3‐day outbreaks, always at the same locations, and resolved spontaneously without residual injury. She had no systemic symptoms, preceding infection, topical exposures, sunburn, bites, animal contacts, or recent medications.

On examination, there were well‐defined, confluent, erythematous papules and plaques with annular, arciform, and polycyclic morphology, central clearing, and purpuric edges. Lesions were symmetrically distributed on the anterior thighs in a mirror‐image pattern.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits, including complete blood count, biochemistry, urinalysis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C‐reactive protein, complement levels (C3, C4, C1q), immunoglobulin levels, rheumatoid factor, and acute‐phase reactants. Antinuclear, anti–double‐stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, anti–Ro, anti–La, and transglutaminase antibodies were negative. Serologies for syphilis, hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and parvovirus B19 were negative. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 40-year-old man presented with a painful nodule on the lower part of his right leg. He reported that the lesion had been stable in size and painless for 4 years but had enlarged and become tender over the past 6 months. There was no history of trauma or personal or family history of malignancy.

On examination, an irregular, firm, erythematous, mobile, tender mass measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm was noted just above the lateral malleolus of the right leg. No popliteal or inguinal lymphadenopathy was present, and there were no other suspicious cutaneous lesions. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, fasting blood sugar, liver and renal function tests, were within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and HIV were negative.

The patient underwent a local excision. Grossly, there was a lobulated, tan-gray, firm mass partly covered by skin, measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm. On light microscopy, the dermal tumor extended into the superficial subcutis and was composed of nests and fascicles of spindle-shaped to epithelioid cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli within a collagenous stroma. Mitotic figures, including atypical forms, measured 7–8 per 10 high-power fields. There was no intracytoplasmic melanin pigment, and the overlying epidermis showed no increase in basal melanocytes, junctional activity, or pagetoid spread.

Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for vimentin and focal positivity for Melan-A and HMB-45. The tumor cells were negative for S-100 protein, pancytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, and CD31.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
An 8-year-old, previously healthy, fully immunized girl presented with 5 days of intermittent fever followed by abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic; her parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms for 1 week. Outpatient oral antibiotics and IV fluids did not improve her symptoms. She was admitted to surgery with suspected appendicitis; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Persistent fever, abdominal pain, and the emergence of a rash and conjunctivitis prompted transfer to the pediatric COVID-19 ward. 

On examination, temperature was 38.6 °C. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and neck demonstrated an 11 × 8.6 × 9.5 cm lobulated solid mass arising from the right thoracic operculum/pleura, with a nodular pleural component, mass effect on the right hilum, supra-aortic vessels, and superior vena cava, pneumomediastinum, left pneumothorax, and lytic destruction with cortical fracture of the T1 and T2 vertebrae. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 13.47 × 10^3/µL (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 303 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.39, lactic acid 2.83 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 4.20 mg/dL, LDH 592 U/L, calcium 6.58 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.73 mg/dL; arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.30, PCO2 44.5 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3 22.3 mmol/L, BE –3.7 mmol/L, and SO2 98%. She received dexamethasone and piperacillin/tazobactam. Given the atypical imaging features and concern for possible hematologic malignancy, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy was planned to obtain adequate tissue.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 37-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with continuous chest pain for two hours. She denied dyspnea, syncope, or prior similar episodes. There was no personal or family history of cardiovascular or thromboembolic disease. Vital signs were: pulse 110/min, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37 °C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air (99% on 2 L/min nasal cannula). Cardiac auscultation was normal, and neck veins were not distended. Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm with 2 mm of ST-segment elevation in leads V2 and V3. She was given aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous heparin and taken to the catheterization laboratory. Twenty minutes later, a second ECG showed a new right bundle branch block and resolution of the precordial ST-segment elevations. Forty-five minutes after presentation, coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries without stenosis. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular dilatation and an estimated pulmonary arterial pressure of 60 mmHg.

A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology.
